title: Quantum key distribution using generalized contextuality against post-quantum eavesdroppers
authors: Daniel Centeno, Roberto D. Baldijão, Maria Ciudad Alañón, Yujie Zhang, Pedro Lauand, Elie Wolfe
abstract: Bell nonlocality allows secret key to be certified without trusting the internal operation of the devices, and even against eavesdroppers constrained only by the no-signaling principle. We ask whether generalized contextuality, a notion of nonclassicality available in prepare-and-measure experiments on a single system, can play an analogous role. In our approach, Alice and Bob first establish operational equivalences among their local preparation and measurement procedures, which are then treated as theory-independent constraints that any physical intervention on the communication channel, including that of an adversary, must respect. Eve is otherwise unrestricted, that is, her intervention on the transmitted system is not assumed to be described by quantum theory. Within this adversarial model, we show that Eve's optimal guessing probability against individual attacks is the solution of a finite linear program, and hence that a worst-case asymptotic key rate follows from the observed statistics and the operational equivalences alone. We prove that contextuality is necessary for a positive key rate. However, we also show that it is not sufficient. Concretely, the (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code, known to yield secret key against a quantum eavesdropper, yields none certifiable key rate against a post-quantum one. Conversely, operational equivalences with no analogue among no-signaling constraints can strictly increase the asymptotic key rate. We illustrate this with the prepare-and-measure version of the standard CHSH protocol with an aligned key-generating setting.
summary: This work analyzes QKD security by replacing the reliance on quantum theory with operational equivalences (OPEQs) derived from local measurements. It proves that generalized contextuality is necessary for a positive key rate against post-quantum eavesdroppers, but it is not sufficient. The study highlights that the operational structure itself, rather than just quantum mechanics, dictates the achievable security rate.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether generalized contextuality, a nonclassicality measure in prepare-and-measure settings, can provide a security guarantee for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) against adversaries who are not restricted by quantum mechanics (post-quantum eavesdroppers).
main_result: Contextuality is proven to be a necessary condition for achieving a positive key rate against such adversaries, but it is not sufficient, as demonstrated by specific counterexamples.
method: The analysis establishes operational equivalences (OPEQs) as theory-independent constraints and formulates the worst-case key rate as a finite linear program over extensions of observed statistics.
model_or_system: The model is a prepare-and-measure QKD scenario where Alice prepares a state and sends it to Bob for measurement. The security analysis is performed against an adversary (Eve) whose intervention is only constrained by the established OPEQs, not by quantum theory.
key_observables: Worst-case asymptotic key rate, generalized contextuality, and operational equivalences.
important_parameters: The key rate is bounded by maximizing Eve's guessing probability over all admissible attacks satisfying the OPEQs.
main_assumptions: The security analysis assumes that local operational equivalences established by Alice and Bob must be respected by any physical intervention on the channel, even by an adversary.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the basic prepare-and-measure QKD setup. Other figures and tables compare key rates for various protocols (like CHSH) under different adversarial constraints.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem by comparing Bell nonlocality to generalized contextuality. It then develops the adversarial model using OPEQs, proving contextuality is necessary. Subsequently, it shows contextuality is not sufficient and concludes by comparing key rates achievable under quantum vs. post-quantum assumptions.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, operational framework for device-independent security that extends beyond standard quantum assumptions, linking fundamental concepts of nonclassicality (contextuality) to practical cryptographic security.
